The money spent on building a new factory.
The value of company stock.
questions.explanation: Working Capital (Current Assets - Current Liabilities) evaluates whether a business can meet its immediate debt obligations.

questions.question: What is Gross Profit vs Net Profit?
options: Gross Profit is Revenue minus Cost of Goods Sold (COGS); Net Profit is the final profit after deducting all operating expenses, interest, and taxes.
Gross profit is after taxes; Net profit is before taxes.
Gross profit only includes cash sales.
They are identical values.
questions.explanation: Gross profit reflects direct production margin; Net profit (the 'bottom line') reflects total company profitability after all operating expenses.

questions.question: What is a General Ledger (GL)?
options: The master set of accounts that summarizes all financial transactions recorded across the business.
A list of company employees.
An address book of customers.
A software manual for accounting tools.
questions.explanation: The General Ledger is the central record-keeping system containing debit and credit transactions categorized by account chart.

questions.question: What is a Trial Balance?
options: A bookkeeping worksheet where the balances of all ledgers are compiled into debit and credit columns to verify mathematical equality.
A trial period where software is free for 30 days.
A bank statement showing interest.
An audit conducted by police.
questions.explanation: The Trial Balance verifies arithmetic accuracy; if total debits equal total credits, the basic math of the books is sound.

questions.question: What is an Invoice in commercial transactions?
options: A time-stamped commercial document issued by a seller to a buyer detailing products, quantities, agreed prices, and payment terms.
A receipt given after payment has already cleared.
A marketing brochure.
A legal contract for hiring employees.
questions.explanation: An invoice requests payment for supplied items, documenting tax compliance (GSTIN, HSN codes) and payment schedules.

questions.question: What does HSN code stand for under GST invoices?
options: Harmonized System of Nomenclature — a standardized numerical code for classifying goods worldwide.
High Security Number
Home State Network
Hourly Salary Number
questions.explanation: HSN is a multi-purpose international naming system developed by the World Customs Organization (WCO) to classify goods for tax rates.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an E-Way Bill in GST compliance for goods transportation?
options: An electronic document generated on the GST portal evidencing the legal movement of goods worth over a threshold (e.g. ₹50,000).
A train ticket for truck drivers.
An online highway toll payment receipt.
An import visa for goods.
questions.explanation: E-Way bills are mandatory digital permits tracking consignment movement to prevent tax evasion across state borders.

skill_quizzes_20.name: Project management basics (Agile, Scrum)
skill_quizzes_20.displayName: Agile Methodologies, Scrum Framework & Project Governance
skill_quizzes_20.description: Agile Manifesto values, Scrum roles, ceremonies, artifacts, Kanban WIP limits, and sprint metrics.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the four foundational core values of the Agile Manifesto?
options: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Comprehensive documentation over working software
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
Following a rigid plan over responding to change
questions.explanation: The Agile Manifesto values: Individuals & interactions over processes; Working software over documentation; Customer collaboration over contracts; Responding to change over plans.

questions.question: In the Scrum framework, what are the three distinct defined roles?
options: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers (Development Team)
Project Manager, Technical Lead, QA Engineer
CEO, CTO, Lead Architect
Business Analyst, Software Developer, System Administrator
questions.explanation: Scrum defines exactly 3 roles: Product Owner (maximizes product value), Scrum Master (coaches process), Developers (build the increment).

questions.question: What is the primary responsibility of the Product Owner in Scrum?
options: Managing and prioritizing the Product Backlog to maximize the value delivered by the team.
Assigning daily coding tasks to developers.
Facilitating daily standup meetings.
Writing all automated unit tests.
questions.explanation: The Product Owner owns the vision, prioritizes features, and ensures the Product Backlog reflects stakeholder value.

questions.question: What is the typical timeboxed duration of a Daily Scrum (Daily Standup) meeting?
options: 15 minutes
1 hour
45 minutes
5 minutes
questions.explanation: The Daily Scrum is strictly timeboxed to 15 minutes to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the daily plan.

questions.question: What are the three questions developers traditionally address during a Daily Standup?
options: What did I do yesterday? What will I do today? Are there any blockers/impediments in my way?
How much budget is left? Who is to blame? Can we go home early?
What code did I delete? What bugs did I write? What is the weather?
What is our stock price? Who wrote this bug? When is lunch?
questions.explanation: The classic standup format inspects yesterday's progress, today's commitments, and any impediments obstructing the team.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of the Sprint Retrospective meeting?
options: For the Scrum Team to inspect how the last Sprint went regarding individuals, interactions, processes, and tools, and identify actionable improvements.
Demonstrating working software to external clients.
Estimating story points for the next 6 months.
Assigning performance bonuses to developers.
questions.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective focuses on continuous team improvement: what went well, what went wrong, and how to improve next sprint.

questions.question: What is the Definition of Done (DoD) in Scrum?
options: A formal shared checklist of quality criteria that a product increment must satisfy before it can be considered complete and releasable.
When a developer finishes typing code on their local laptop.
When the Product Owner leaves the office for the day.
When the sprint deadline clock reaches midnight.
questions.explanation: The DoD ensures transparency by establishing a shared standard of quality (e.g. tested, reviewed, documented, passing CI/CD).

questions.question: What is a Sprint Burndown Chart used for?
options: Showing the remaining work (story points or hours) across the days of the Sprint to track progress toward the Sprint Goal.
Calculating the financial burn rate of company bank accounts.
Measuring CPU heat on the build server.
Recording lines of code deleted.
questions.explanation: A burndown chart visualizes remaining sprint backlog work over time, highlighting whether the team is on track to complete commitments.

questions.question: In Kanban, what is the primary purpose of a 'Work In Progress' (WIP) Limit?
options: Restricting the maximum number of task cards allowed in any workflow state to prevent bottlenecks and improve flow throughput.
Limiting how many hours a developer can work per week.
Limiting the number of lines of code in a file.
Preventing new employees from joining the project.
questions.explanation: WIP limits prevent multitasking and context-switching, forcing teams to complete existing work before starting new items.

questions.question: What is a User Story typically composed of in Agile requirements management?
options: A short template: 'As a <type of user>, I want <goal/feature>, so that <business value/benefit>'.
A 50-page technical specification document.
A database schema diagram.
A financial balance sheet.
questions.explanation: User stories capture software requirements from the end-user's perspective, emphasizing business value.

questions.question: What are Story Points in Agile estimation?
options: A relative unit of measure assessing the overall effort, complexity, and uncertainty of a user story rather than raw calendar hours.
Loyalty points earned by developers.
The number of words in a user story.
The hourly billing rate charged to clients.
questions.explanation: Story points evaluate relative size and complexity (often using modified Fibonacci: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) independent of specific hourly estimations.

questions.question: What is Team Velocity in Scrum?
options: The average amount of Product Backlog work (in story points) completed and verified as 'Done' by the team during a typical Sprint.
The internet upload speed of the office Wi-Fi.
The typing speed of developers in words per minute.
The speed of server deployment pipelines.
questions.explanation: Velocity measures the pace of delivery across sprints, helping the team forecast realistic capacity for future sprint planning.

questions.question: What is the Sprint Backlog?
options: The set of Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint, along with the plan for delivering the product Increment.
All ideas the company will build over the next 5 years.
A list of bugs that cannot be fixed.
An archive of deleted files.
questions.explanation: The Sprint Backlog is owned by the developers and represents the specific items committed to achieving the Sprint Goal.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the Scrum Master?
options: A servant-leader who coaches the team on Scrum principles, facilitates events, and removes organizational impediments.
The authoritarian boss who assigns tasks to developers.
The lead programmer who writes the most code.
The client representative paying the bills.
questions.explanation: The Scrum Master is a servant leader focused on team effectiveness, removing blockers, and fostering high-performance agile culture.

questions.question: What occurs during the Sprint Review meeting?
options: The Scrum Team presents the completed working Increment to stakeholders and discusses what to build next.
The team conducts code refactoring in private.
The manager reviews developer attendance.
The team plans the next sprint's detailed tasks.
questions.explanation: The Sprint Review is a collaborative session where the team demonstrates the completed increment to stakeholders to gather feedback.

questions.question: What is the INVEST mnemonic used for in Agile requirements?
options: Criteria for quality user stories: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
A guide on how to invest venture capital money.
A formula for calculating interest on bank loans.
An acronym for corporate budgeting.
questions.explanation: Bill Wake's INVEST criteria ensures stories are ready for sprint execution: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

questions.question: What is a 'Spike' in Agile terminology?
options: A timeboxed research or exploratory task aimed at gathering information or resolving technical uncertainty before estimating a feature.
A sudden crash in server memory.
A sharp increase in company sales.
An argument during a meeting.
questions.explanation: A spike is a timeboxed investigation used when the team needs to explore architecture, test a library, or reduce risk before committing.

questions.question: What is the difference between Scrum and Waterfall project management?
options: Waterfall is linear, sequential, and phase-based with heavy upfront planning; Scrum is iterative, incremental, and adapts to changing requirements.
Waterfall only uses computers; Scrum uses paper cards.
Scrum has no testing phase.
Waterfall has no project managers.
questions.explanation: Waterfall flows sequentially from requirements to design to implementation to testing; Scrum delivers working increments iteratively.

questions.question: What is 'Scope Creep'?
options: The uncontrolled expansion of project scope without adjustments to time, cost, or resources.
A developer working on code at midnight.
Zooming in on a user interface screen.
A bug moving from one file to another.
questions.explanation: Scope creep happens when new features and requirements are continuously added without adjusting project deadlines or budgets.

questions.question: What is a Gantt Chart primarily used for in traditional project management?
options: Illustrating a project schedule, displaying task dependencies, start and finish dates, and milestones along a visual timeline.
Calculating company tax liabilities.
Listing database tables.
Evaluating developer typing speeds.
questions.explanation: A Gantt chart illustrates project activities as horizontal bars plotted against a timeline, showing task sequences and dependencies.

skill_quizzes.name: SQL basics
skill_quizzes.description: DDL/DML queries, SELECT filters, JOIN operations, GROUP BY, aggregations, and constraints.

questions.question: Which SQL keyword is used to retrieve only unique values from a column?
options: DISTINCT
UNIQUE
DIFFERENT
FILTER
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the query output.

questions.question: Which SQL clause is used to filter records after an aggregate function (e.g., COUNT or SUM) is computed?
options: WHERE
HAVING
GROUP FILTER
ORDER BY
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups created by GROUP BY; WHERE filters rows before aggregation.

questions.question: Which type of JOIN returns all records from the left table and matched records from the right table?
options: INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN
RIGHT JOIN
FULL OUTER JOIN
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN (or LEFT OUTER JOIN) returns all rows from the left table and matched rows from the right table (NULL if no match).

questions.question: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE in SQL?
options: DELETE removes the table structure; TRUNCATE only removes rows.
TRUNCATE is a DDL command that resets identity counters and cannot be selectively filtered by a WHERE clause; DELETE is DML and can use WHERE.
TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back under any circumstance, whereas DELETE cannot be logged.
Both perform identical physical page reclamation in all relational engines.
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE quickly empties a table by deallocating pages and does not accept a WHERE clause; DELETE deletes rows one by one and accepts WHERE.

questions.question: Which SQL constraint uniquely identifies each row in a database table and disallows NULL values?
options: FOREIGN KEY
UNIQUE
PRIMARY KEY
CHECK
questions.explanation: A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each record in a table and must not contain NULL values.

questions.question: What does the SQL command 'ROLLBACK' do during a transaction?
options: Permanently saves all pending changes to the disk.
Undoes all changes made within the current uncommitted transaction.
Restores the database to its initial installation state.
Deletes the latest index created.
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK reverts all database modifications made within the active transaction prior to a COMMIT.

questions.question: Which wildcard character in SQL LIKE operator represents zero, one, or multiple characters?
questions.explanation: In SQL LIKE clauses, '%' matches zero or more characters; '_' matches exactly one character.

questions.question: Which aggregate function calculates the total number of non-null rows matching a criteria?
options: SUM()
COUNT()
TOTAL()
AVG()
questions.explanation: COUNT(column) counts non-null occurrences of that column; COUNT(*) counts all matching rows.

questions.question: How do you sort a query result in descending order by the 'created_at' column?
options: ORDER BY created_at DESC
SORT BY created_at DESC
GROUP BY created_at DOWN
FILTER BY created_at DESCENDING
questions.explanation: ORDER BY column_name DESC sorts results from highest to lowest.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a database INDEX?
options: To enforce referential integrity between parent and child tables.
To accelerate data retrieval operations (SELECTs) at the expense of slower write operations.
To compress disk storage by 50%.
To automatically encrypt sensitive database columns.
questions.explanation: An index (such as B-Tree) provides fast lookups without scanning every row, though it requires overhead during INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

questions.question: What will the expression 'SELECT NULL = NULL' evaluate to in SQL standard?
options: TRUE
FALSE
UNKNOWN / NULL
ERROR
questions.explanation: In three-valued SQL logic, NULL cannot equal NULL; you must use 'IS NULL' or 'IS NOT NULL'.

questions.question: Which SQL keyword is used to restrict the number of rows returned in PostgreSQL and MySQL?
options: TOP
LIMIT
ROWNUM
RESTRICT
questions.explanation: LIMIT specifies the maximum number of rows to return (e.g., LIMIT 10).

questions.question: What is a FOREIGN KEY used for?
options: Connecting to an external cloud database server.
Enforcing referential integrity by linking a column to the primary key of another table.
Storing international currency values.
Automatically converting character sets.
questions.explanation: A FOREIGN KEY ensures that values in a child table match an existing valid primary key in the referenced parent table.

questions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
options: UNION eliminates duplicate rows; UNION ALL includes all rows including duplicates.
UNION only works with numbers; UNION ALL works with strings.
UNION ALL is slower because it sorts data in memory.
There is no functional difference between them.
questions.explanation: UNION performs an internal distinct sorting operation to eliminate duplicate rows, while UNION ALL simply concatenates result sets without deduplication.

questions.question: Which DML statement is used to modify existing data in a table?
options: ALTER
MODIFY
UPDATE
CHANGE
questions.explanation: UPDATE table_name SET col = val WHERE condition is used to modify existing row values.

questions.question: What is the result of applying GROUP BY on a column?
options: It groups identical column values into summary rows so aggregate functions can be applied.
It permanently re-sorts table rows on the disk storage.
It deletes all rows that have duplicate keys.
It creates a virtual foreign key relationship.
questions.explanation: GROUP BY summarizes rows with identical values into single rows for computing aggregates like COUNT, SUM, or AVG.

questions.question: Which clause is used to combine conditions where AT LEAST ONE condition must be true?
options: AND
OR
BOTH
EITHER
questions.explanation: OR evaluates to true if either condition is true.

questions.question: What does ACID stand for in database management systems?
options: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Accuracy, Concurrency, Indexing, Data
Availability, Consistency, Integrity, Durability
Asynchronous, Coherent, Isolated, Distributed
questions.explanation: ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) guarantee reliable transaction processing in relational databases.

questions.question: What is a SQL View?
options: A physical copy of table data stored in RAM.
A virtual table based on the result-set of a stored SQL query.
A tool used only for generating graphical charts.
An encrypted backup file on cloud storage.
questions.explanation: A View contains no physical data of its own; it dynamically executes a predefined query whenever referenced.

questions.question: Which SQL statement is used to remove an entire table including its schema and definitions from the database?
options: DELETE TABLE
DROP TABLE
REMOVE TABLE
TRUNCATE SCHEMA
questions.explanation: DROP TABLE table_name permanently removes both the data and the table definition from the database catalog.

skill_quizzes.name: HTTP & REST
skill_quizzes.description: HTTP verbs, response status codes, statelessness, headers, idempotency, and RESTful resource modeling.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code should be returned when a new resource is successfully created via a POST request?
options: 200 OK
201 Created
204 No Content
202 Accepted
questions.explanation: 201 Created is the standard HTTP response indicating successful resource creation.

questions.question: What does it mean for an HTTP method to be 'idempotent'?
options: The method cannot be cached by intermediate proxies.
Executing the request multiple times produces the exact same server state as executing it once.
The request must always return an empty response body.
The request can only be transmitted over HTTPS.
questions.explanation: An idempotent method (like GET, PUT, DELETE) can be called multiple times without altering the final server state beyond the initial call.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural difference between PUT and PATCH in RESTful APIs?
options: PUT replaces the entire resource representation; PATCH applies partial modifications.
PATCH is idempotent whereas PUT is non-idempotent.
PUT cannot include a request body; PATCH requires URL parameters.
PATCH is only supported in HTTP/3.
questions.explanation: PUT represents a full replacement of the resource; PATCH applies partial updates to specific fields.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code represents 'Unauthorized' (authentication required or invalid credentials)?
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized indicates that the request lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource.

questions.question: What is the key difference between status codes 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
options: 401 means the client identity is not authenticated; 403 means the identity is known but lacks permission/authorization.
401 applies to GET requests; 403 applies to POST requests.
401 indicates server failure; 403 indicates client DNS failure.
They are interchangeable synonyms in the HTTP specification.
questions.explanation: 401 represents an authentication failure (who are you?), while 403 represents an authorization failure (you cannot access this resource).

questions.question: What does HTTP 'statelessness' mean?
options: The server retains client memory across requests without tokens.
Every request from client to server must contain all the information necessary to understand and process the request.
The server must not store any data in a relational database.
The API must run purely in serverless containers without disk.
questions.explanation: In a stateless protocol, the server stores no session context about the client between requests; every request must carry its own authorization and state.

questions.question: Which HTTP response code indicates that an operation succeeded but returns no response body?
options: 200 OK
201 Created
204 No Content
304 Not Modified
questions.explanation: 204 No Content confirms that the server has fulfilled the request and that there is no additional content to send in the payload.

questions.question: Which HTTP header is used by the client to inform the server of the media type of the request body being sent?
options: Accept
Content-Type
User-Agent
Authorization
questions.explanation: Content-Type specifies the MIME type of the payload being transmitted (e.g., application/json).

questions.question: Which HTTP header is sent by the client to indicate which content types it can understand in the response?
options: Accept
Content-Type
Content-Encoding
Host
questions.explanation: The Accept request header advertises which content types the client is able to process (e.g., Accept: application/json).

questions.question: What is CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)?
options: A database clustering protocol for multi-region replication.
A browser security mechanism that allows or restricts resources requested from another origin.
An encryption standard replacing SSL certificates.
A load balancer algorithm for distributing traffic.
questions.explanation: CORS is an HTTP-header based browser security mechanism allowing a server to indicate any origins other than its own from which a browser should permit loading resources.

questions.question: Which HTTP method should be used to safely read or retrieve data without causing side effects on the server?
options: GET
POST
DELETE
PATCH
questions.explanation: GET is defined as a 'safe' method by RFC 7231, meaning it is intended only for information retrieval and causes no side effects.

questions.question: What status code category represents server-side errors?
options: 2xx
3xx
4xx
5xx
questions.explanation: 5xx status codes (such as 500, 502, 503, 504) represent server-side internal errors.

questions.question: What is the recommended RESTful URL pattern for retrieving a specific book with ID 42 from a collection?
options: /get_book?id=42
/books/42
/bookAction/retrieve/42
/books.php?select=42
questions.explanation: REST design uses plural nouns for collections and resource identifiers in the path: /books/{id}.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the HTTP 'ETag' header?
options: Assigning a unique tracking identifier to every user.
An identifier for a specific version of a resource used for web cache validation and conditional requests.
Enforcing password complexity rules.
Compressing image assets in the payload.
questions.explanation: An ETag (entity tag) allows caches to be more efficient and saves bandwidth when the content has not changed (via If-None-Match).

questions.question: What status code is returned when a client sends an invalid request, such as malformed JSON syntax?
options: 400 Bad Request
404 Not Found
405 Method Not Allowed
500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation: 400 Bad Request indicates that the server cannot process the request due to perceived client error (e.g., malformed syntax).

questions.question: What is the function of the HTTP 301 status code?
options: Temporary Redirect
Moved Permanently
Found
See Other
questions.explanation: 301 Moved Permanently tells clients and search engine crawlers that the target resource has been permanently assigned a new URI.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is specifically used during CORS preflight checks by web browsers?
options: HEAD
OPTIONS
TRACE
CONNECT
questions.explanation: Browsers send an OPTIONS request before certain cross-origin requests to verify permitted methods and headers.

questions.question: What is the purpose of HTTP Query Parameters (e.g., /users?role=developer&page=2)?
options: Filtering, sorting, and paginating collection resources.
Encrypting payload content.
Modifying the database schema.
Specifying the SSL cipher algorithm.
questions.explanation: Query parameters are primarily used for searching, sorting, filtering, and paginating collection items.

questions.question: What status code should be returned when a requested route or endpoint does not exist?
questions.explanation: 404 Not Found indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2?
options: HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexing over a single TCP connection, eliminating head-of-line blocking.
HTTP/2 removes headers and only transmits raw bytes.
HTTP/2 requires relational SQL databases to operate.
HTTP/2 cannot transmit JSON objects.
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 introduces binary framing and request/response multiplexing over a single TCP connection to drastically improve page load speed.

skill_quizzes.name: Databases (relational vs NoSQL)
skill_quizzes.description: ACID vs BASE, schema models, document vs key-value vs graph stores, normalization, scaling, and CAP theorem.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference in data modeling between relational databases and Document NoSQL databases?
options: Relational databases use rigid tabular schemas with foreign keys; Document NoSQL databases store semi-structured records (JSON/BSON).
NoSQL databases cannot store numbers.
Relational databases cannot perform mathematical queries.
Document databases do not permit reading data.
questions.explanation: Relational DBs (PostgreSQL, MySQL, HANA) enforce schema tables with relations; Document DBs (MongoDB) store flexible JSON-like documents.

questions.question: What does the CAP theorem state regarding distributed data systems?
options: A distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance.
A database must always prioritize Speed over Accuracy.
Any database can provide 100% Consistency, Availability, and Partitioning simultaneously under network failure.
Cloud systems never experience network partitions.
questions.explanation: The CAP theorem proves that in the event of a network partition (P), a distributed system must choose between Consistency (C) and Availability (A).

questions.question: Which database type is Redis primarily categorized as?
options: In-memory Key-Value store
Document Store
Graph Database
Relational OLAP Database
questions.explanation: Redis is an open-source, in-memory data structure store used primarily as a fast key-value cache and message broker.

questions.question: What type of NoSQL database is Neo4j?
options: Document Database
Columnar Database
Graph Database
Key-Value Database
questions.explanation: Neo4j is a Graph database designed specifically for interconnected data models (nodes, relationships, properties).

questions.question: What is 'Database Normalization' primarily intended to achieve in relational design?
options: Minimize data redundancy and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.
Increase file size on disk for redundancy.
Convert all relational tables into raw JSON text.
Make all query operations unindexed.
questions.explanation: Normalization organizes fields and tables to reduce duplicate data (redundancy) and prevent anomalies.

questions.question: What is Horizontal Scaling (Sharding) in database systems?
options: Adding more CPU, RAM, or SSD to a single server instance.
Distributing data across multiple independent server nodes.
Converting table columns into rows.
Enforcing foreign key constraints on every column.
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale-out / sharding) partitions data across multiple machines, whereas vertical scaling (scale-up) adds power to one machine.

questions.question: What does BASE stand for in NoSQL distributed architectures?
options: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
Binary Architecture, Synchronous Execution
Basic Access, Standard Encryption
Buffered Allocations, Scalable Entities
questions.explanation: BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) models trade immediate strong consistency for higher availability and partition tolerance.

questions.question: When is a NoSQL Document Store (like MongoDB) typically preferred over a strict relational database?
options: When data structures are rapidly evolving and hierarchical/nested documents map naturally to application objects.
When processing double-entry financial accounting ledger transactions requiring multi-table strict foreign keys.
When database queries only involve mathematical matrix multiplication.
When data must strictly adhere to third normal form (3NF).
questions.explanation: Document databases excel when working with polymorphic, semi-structured, or rapidly evolving JSON payloads without migrations.

questions.question: What is a Read Replica used for?
options: Handling write and delete operations exclusively.
Offloading read-heavy query traffic from the primary master database node.
Compressing backup files into zip format.
Managing user authorization sessions.
questions.explanation: Read replicas replicate data from the primary node to serve read traffic asynchronously, preventing saturation of the write master.

questions.question: Which NoSQL category does Apache Cassandra belong to?
options: Wide-column / Column-family store
Graph store
Document store
Relational database
questions.explanation: Apache Cassandra is a distributed wide-column store designed for massive write throughput across multi-datacenter clusters.

questions.question: What is 'Eventual Consistency'?
options: The guarantee that if no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually return the latest value.
The guarantee that data will never be consistent across nodes.
A guarantee that every read operation is permanently blocked until written.
A concept found only in relational SQL databases.
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency guarantees that all replicas will converge to the same value given sufficient time without updates.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of over-normalizing a relational database (e.g., beyond 3NF)?
options: Queries require numerous complex JOIN operations, degrading read query performance.
The database can no longer store strings.
Foreign keys are permanently disabled.
The database cannot be backed up.
questions.explanation: Excessive normalization splits data into many small tables, requiring expensive multi-table JOINs for simple read lookups.

questions.question: What is Denormalization?
options: Purposely introducing redundancy into a database to optimize read performance and reduce JOINs.
Corrupting the database index files.
Deleting all primary keys in a table.
Converting relational schemas into raw text files.
questions.explanation: Denormalization deliberately combines data to improve read query performance at the cost of some write redundancy.

questions.question: What is a Database Transaction?
options: A sequence of database operations treated as a single indivisible unit of work.
A monetary fee paid to a cloud provider per query.
A single SELECT query with no parameters.
A network packet sent between client and server.
questions.explanation: A transaction bundles multiple operations so they either all succeed together or all fail together (Atomicity).

questions.question: What is Connection Pooling in database architectures?
options: Maintaining a cache of open database connections that can be reused for subsequent requests.
Connecting two separate databases using a network cable.
Merging all user queries into a single SQL file.
Storing database backups in a shared data lake.
questions.explanation: Connection pooling avoids the significant latency and resource overhead of establishing a new TCP/TLS connection for every single query.

questions.question: Which database model is optimal for social networks and recommendation engines showing mutual friendships?
options: Graph Database
Flat File CSV
Key-Value Store
Relational Database with 20 JOINs
questions.explanation: Graph databases (like Neo4j) traverse relationships (edges) between entities (nodes) in constant time without multi-table JOIN bottlenecks.

questions.question: What is 'Schema-on-Read'?
options: Data is stored in raw format, and the structure is applied only when the data is read by an application.
Data must strictly conform to a predefined schema before being inserted into disk.
The database reads the schema every millisecond to update indexes.
A technique exclusive to SQLite.
questions.explanation: Schema-on-read formats raw data dynamically during query execution (typical of data lakes and NoSQL), unlike schema-on-write (RDBMS).

questions.question: What is Database Sharding?
options: Partitioning a very large database horizontally across multiple servers based on a shard key.
Compressing table data into smaller disk blocks.
Encrypting data using hash algorithms.
Rebuilding primary keys after server restart.
questions.explanation: Sharding distributes rows of a table across multiple database nodes based on a partition/shard key.

questions.question: What does 'Time-to-Live' (TTL) in a Key-Value database (e.g. Redis) indicate?
options: The time duration before a key is automatically expired and deleted from memory.
The lifespan of the physical server hardware.
The network latency round-trip time.
The time taken to write a backup to disk.
questions.explanation: TTL configures a lifespan after which a key automatically expires, ideal for session tokens and caching.

questions.question: Which relational database engine is embedded directly into client applications without a standalone server daemon?
options: SQLite
PostgreSQL
Oracle 21c
Microsoft SQL Server
questions.explanation: SQLite is a lightweight, serverless, self-contained SQL database engine embedded directly into mobile and desktop applications.

skill_quizzes.name: Cloud basics (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS)
skill_quizzes.displayName: Cloud Fundamentals (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS & Shared Responsibility)
skill_quizzes.description: Cloud service models, Capex vs Opex, shared responsibility, regions, availability zones, and virtualization.

questions.question: Which cloud service model provides virtualized computing resources (virtual machines, storage, and networks) where the customer manages the OS, middleware, and applications?
options: SaaS
PaaS
IaaS
FaaS
questions.explanation: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS, e.g. Amazon EC2, Azure VMs, Google Compute Engine) leaves OS and application management to the user.

questions.question: Which cloud model allows developers to deploy code without managing the underlying operating system, server hardware, or runtime patches?
options: IaaS
PaaS
Hardware as a Service
On-Premises Data Center
questions.explanation: Platform as a Service (PaaS, e.g. SAP BTP, Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk) manages the OS, runtime, and infrastructure so developers only focus on code.

questions.question: Which category does Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or Salesforce represent?
options: IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
BaaS
questions.explanation: Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers complete end-user software applications managed entirely by the provider.

questions.question: What is the Shared Responsibility Model in cloud computing?
options: The division of security and operational responsibilities between the cloud provider and the cloud customer.
Sharing cloud subscription costs among multiple employees.
A contract where two competing cloud vendors share the same physical server.
Requiring two passwords to access the cloud console.
questions.explanation: The provider is responsible for security 'of' the cloud (hardware, facilities); the customer is responsible for security 'in' the cloud (data, access, configuration).

questions.question: What financial transition does cloud computing enable by replacing upfront data center purchases with pay-as-you-go pricing?
options: Shifting from CapEx (Capital Expenditure) to OpEx (Operational Expenditure).
Shifting from OpEx to CapEx.
Eliminating all operational costs permanently.
Converting taxes into hardware assets.
questions.explanation: Cloud models reduce large upfront Capital Expenditures (CapEx) on servers and replace them with variable, ongoing Operational Expenditures (OpEx).

questions.question: What is a Cloud Availability Zone (AZ)?
options: One or more discrete physical data centers with redundant power, networking, and cooling within a geographic Region.
The entire continent where a cloud provider operates.
A software container deployed on a client laptop.
A backup hard drive stored in a vault.
questions.explanation: An Availability Zone is an isolated data center location within a Region engineered to be resilient against local failures.

questions.question: What is Cloud Elasticity?
options: The ability to dynamically scale computing resources up or down automatically based on real-time workload demands.
The physical flexibility of server cables.
The capacity to run code on any operating system without changes.
An SLA metric for network cables.
questions.explanation: Elasticity allows systems to automatically adapt capacity to match current demand, avoiding over-provisioning or downtime.

questions.question: What is a 'Public Cloud'?
options: Cloud infrastructure owned and operated by a third-party provider, delivering computing resources over the public internet to multiple tenants.
A government-only supercomputer accessible to all citizens.
A computer network with zero password protection.
A free website hosting platform with no commercial services.
questions.explanation: Public clouds (AWS, Azure, GCP, SAP) share pooled hardware across multiple customer organizations securely via virtualization.

questions.question: What is a 'Hybrid Cloud' architecture?
options: An environment combining on-premises private infrastructure with one or more public cloud services, connected seamlessly.
A data center powered exclusively by wind and solar power.
An app running on both Android and iOS.
A computer with two CPU processors.
questions.explanation: A hybrid cloud binds on-premises private data centers with public cloud infrastructure for workload mobility and data governance.

questions.question: Under the IaaS shared responsibility model, who is responsible for applying operating system security patches to a virtual machine?
options: The cloud customer
The cloud provider
The hardware manufacturer
The internet service provider
questions.explanation: In IaaS, the customer chooses and controls the guest operating system, making OS-level security patching the customer's responsibility.

questions.question: What is 'Multi-Tenancy' in cloud architecture?
options: A single physical instance of software and hardware serving multiple separate customer organizations (tenants) with logical isolation.
A user having multiple cloud passwords.
A tenant renting multiple physical buildings.
Deploying a separate physical server for every individual user.
questions.explanation: Multi-tenancy allows cloud systems to share underlying hardware across multiple distinct customers while maintaining strict data isolation.

questions.question: What is Serverless Computing (Function-as-a-Service / FaaS)?
options: Execution of code where the cloud provider dynamically manages server provisioning, scaling, and billing occurs strictly per invocation/millisecond.
Computing that does not use any physical computers in the universe.
A server running with no operating system.
A private mainframe installed in an office basement.
questions.explanation: In serverless (e.g. AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions), developers write event-driven code without provisioning servers, paying only for execution time.

questions.question: What is a Cloud Region?
options: A distinct geographic area containing multiple, isolated Availability Zones interconnected by low-latency networks.
A single server rack in a computer room.
An entire country with one data center.
A software license jurisdiction.
questions.explanation: A Region (e.g., us-east-1, eu-central-1) represents a physical geographic zone containing several isolated data centers (AZs).

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of deploying an application across Multi-Availability Zones (Multi-AZ)?
options: High availability and fault tolerance against data center outages.
Reducing network bandwidth to zero.
Eliminating the need for software testing.
Making code run twice as fast automatically.
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ deployment ensures that if a fire, flood, or power loss impacts one data center, the secondary AZ takes over traffic immediately.

questions.question: Which metric in a Cloud Service Level Agreement (SLA) measures 'five nines' availability?
options: 99.999% uptime (less than 5.26 minutes downtime per year)
95.555% uptime
99.9% uptime (8.76 hours downtime)
90% uptime
questions.explanation: 'Five nines' (99.999%) represents high-availability enterprise tolerance permitting at most ~5 minutes of unscheduled outage per year.

questions.question: What is Cloud Vendor Lock-In?
options: The difficulty and expense of migrating applications and data from one cloud provider to another due to proprietary APIs and services.
Being locked out of a cloud account due to forgotten password.
A physical door lock on server cages.
An annual maintenance contract with no software updates.
questions.explanation: Vendor lock-in occurs when an organization heavily uses proprietary features of a single vendor that are incompatible with competitors.

questions.question: What role does a Hypervisor play in cloud virtualization?
options: Software that creates and runs multiple virtual machines by sharing physical host hardware resources.
A network router that connects internet cables.
A specialized monitor for system administrators.
An encryption key generator for cloud storage.
questions.explanation: A hypervisor (e.g., KVM, VMware ESXi, Hyper-V) isolates and manages virtual machines on physical host hardware.

questions.question: Which cloud computing deployment model is operated solely for a single organization, whether managed internally or by a third party?
options: Private Cloud
Public Cloud
Community Cloud
Social Cloud
questions.explanation: A Private Cloud provides dedicated infrastructure solely for one organization, often for regulatory or compliance requirements.

questions.question: Under SaaS (Software as a Service), what is the customer responsible for managing?
options: Customer data and user access permissions
Operating system kernel updates
Physical network switches
Data center cooling
questions.explanation: In SaaS, the vendor manages infrastructure, operating systems, and application code; the customer only configures user access and their own data.

questions.question: What is Cloud FinOps?
options: The operational and cultural framework of bringing financial accountability to the variable spend model of cloud computing.
A financial software tool for filing taxes.
A crypto-currency used for cloud bills.
A banking institution specializing in technology loans.
questions.explanation: FinOps combines engineering, finance, and business teams to optimize cloud costs and maintain budgetary governance.

skill_quizzes.name: Cloud storage & scaling
skill_quizzes.displayName: Cloud Storage & Scaling (Block, Object, Elastic Scaling)
skill_quizzes.description: Object vs block vs file storage, S3 buckets, horizontal/vertical scaling, auto-scaling groups, and load balancers.

questions.question: Which storage type is Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage categorized as?
options: Block Storage
Object Storage
File Storage (NFS)
Direct-Attached RAM
questions.explanation: Object storage stores data as discrete objects with metadata and a globally unique key, accessible via HTTP/REST APIs.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between Block Storage (e.g. AWS EBS) and Object Storage (e.g. AWS S3)?
options: Block storage behaves like a raw unformatted physical hard disk attachable to a single VM; Object storage stores complete immutable objects accessible over HTTP.
Block storage cannot be partitioned.
Object storage is only suitable for running operating system boot disks.
Block storage has infinite automatic global replication across all continents.
questions.explanation: Block storage is mounted as virtual disk blocks for operating systems and databases; object storage is flat, infinitely scalable HTTP-accessible storage.

questions.question: What is Vertical Scaling (Scaling Up)?
options: Adding more compute power (CPU, RAM, GPU) to an existing single server instance.
Adding more servers into an auto-scaling cluster.
Storing files vertically on disk tracks.
Connecting servers with taller Ethernet cables.
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling increases the capacity of an individual server instance, up to physical hardware limits.

questions.question: What is Horizontal Scaling (Scaling Out)?
options: Adding more server instances to distribute workload across a fleet.
Upgrading a single VM from 4 CPU cores to 64 CPU cores.
Formatting disks with wider sectors.
Decreasing network bandwidth to reduce latency.
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling adds more instances of a resource (e.g., adding 5 more web servers behind a load balancer).

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an Application Load Balancer (ALB) operating at Layer 7?
options: Distributing incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic based on request headers, path routes, and methods across a target group of servers.
Compressing video files before saving to disk.
Providing physical electricity to server racks.
Enforcing SQL primary key uniqueness.
questions.explanation: Layer 7 load balancers inspect application-layer HTTP traffic to route requests intelligently by URL path, host header, or query parameters.

questions.question: What does an Auto-Scaling Group (ASG) do in cloud architecture?
options: Automatically launches or terminates VM instances based on defined metrics like CPU utilization or request count.
Automatically increases font size on web pages.
Purchases new hardware from vendors via credit card.
Forces all database tables to double their row count.
questions.explanation: Auto-scaling groups monitor metrics (e.g. CPU > 70%) to automatically scale capacity in or out, ensuring availability and cost efficiency.

questions.question: What is a Content Delivery Network (CDN) used for?
options: Caching static and dynamic web content on geographically distributed edge servers close to end users to reduce latency.
Running relational database transactions.
Generating cryptographic private keys.
Creating physical backups on tape drives.
questions.explanation: CDNs (e.g. Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront) cache assets near users geographically to dramatically speed up content delivery.

questions.question: What is the typical durability guarantee of standard Amazon S3 storage class?
questions.explanation: S3 standard provides 99.999999999% annual durability by redundantly storing objects across multiple physical devices and availability zones.

questions.question: When should 'Cold Storage' or 'Archive Storage' (e.g., S3 Glacier) be selected?
options: For infrequently accessed data that requires long-term retention (e.g., compliance records) where retrieval delay of minutes/hours is acceptable.
For high-speed database transaction log files updated 1,000 times per second.
For delivering live video streaming to mobile apps.
For running live web server operating systems.
questions.explanation: Cold/Archive storage offers extremely low storage cost in exchange for longer retrieval times (minutes to hours).

questions.question: What is a Stateless Application Architecture in horizontal scaling?
options: Application servers do not store client session data locally, allowing any incoming request to be handled by any server instance.
The application contains no business logic.
The app cannot interact with a database.
The code has no variable declarations.
questions.explanation: Stateless servers store session state externally (e.g. in Redis or client JWTs), making horizontal scaling simple and seamless.

questions.question: What does a Load Balancer 'Health Check' do?
options: Periodically probes target server endpoints (e.g. GET /health) and stops routing traffic to instances that fail to respond correctly.
Measures physical room temperature in data centers.
Checks the operating system license expiration date.
Validates the grammar of web page text.
questions.explanation: Health checks ensure traffic is only routed to healthy, responsive instances, automatically bypassing failing nodes.

questions.question: What is the role of File Storage (e.g. AWS EFS, Azure Files, NFS) in the cloud?
options: Shared file system storage that can be mounted concurrently by multiple virtual machines over the network.
Storage limited strictly to single-core CPUs.
Direct-attached RAM disk for graphics cards.
A local browser cookie storage engine.
questions.explanation: Network File Storage (NFS/SMB) provides hierarchical file system access shareable simultaneously across multiple compute nodes.

questions.question: What is Edge Computing?
options: Deploying compute workloads geographically closer to the data source or end user to minimize network round-trip latency.
Using only the edges of physical circuit boards.
Writing code on the borders of terminal windows.
A technique exclusive to satellite communication.
questions.explanation: Edge computing processes data near the network edge where things or people produce and consume that data.

questions.question: What is Storage Tiering (Lifecycle Management)?
options: Automatically migrating objects to cheaper storage tiers (e.g., from Standard to Infrequent Access to Archive) as data ages.
Formatting hard drives into tiers of physical sectors.
Purchasing storage subscriptions in 3-year increments.
Encrypting files with multi-tier passwords.
questions.explanation: Lifecycle rules automatically transition objects between storage tiers based on age to optimize cloud storage expenditure.

questions.question: What is a major challenge when scaling a Stateful application horizontally?
options: Maintaining synchronized persistent state and session consistency across all running nodes.
Writing CSS code.
Connecting servers to the internet.
Creating user accounts in Git.
questions.explanation: Stateful systems (like distributed databases) must coordinate consensus, replication, and data locking across all nodes.

questions.question: What is Elastic Block Store (EBS) snapshotting?
options: Point-in-time incremental backups of a block storage volume saved into object storage (S3).
A camera photograph of a physical server rack.
A screenshot of a terminal window.
A temporary cache in browser memory.
questions.explanation: Snapshots provide incremental point-in-time volume backups, copying only the blocks that changed since the last snapshot.

questions.question: What is a Sticky Session (Session Affinity) on a load balancer?
options: Routing all requests from a specific client to the same backend server instance for the duration of a session.
Preventing users from logging out of an application.
A session that permanently locks server CPU.
A network protocol used for hardware testing.
questions.explanation: Sticky sessions bind a user's session to a specific instance, often used as a workaround for legacy stateful applications.

questions.question: What is Network Attached Storage (NAS)?
options: File-level computer data storage connected to a computer network providing data access to a heterogeneous group of clients.
An internal motherboard bus connecting CPU to RAM.
A wireless router with no hard drive.
A direct optical cable between two satellites.
questions.explanation: NAS provides file-level data access to networked clients using protocols such as NFS or SMB.

questions.question: What is Storage Encryption at Rest?
options: Encrypting data while it is stored on physical media (disks, tapes, flash) to prevent unauthorized access if the media is compromised.
Encrypting data only when transmitted over HTTPS cables.
Deleting data when a computer enters sleep mode.
Compressing files to reduce disk size.
questions.explanation: Encryption at rest safeguards data stored on disks using algorithms like AES-256 with managed cryptographic keys.

questions.question: What is Cross-Region Replication (CRR) in object storage?
options: Automatically copying uploaded objects across buckets in different geographic regions for disaster recovery and compliance.
Copying files across folders on the same computer.
Renaming files every hour.
Sending database queries across two terminal windows.
questions.explanation: CRR asynchronously replicates objects across different geographic cloud regions for low-latency multi-region access and disaster recovery.

skill_quizzes.name: Linux basics
skill_quizzes.displayName: Linux Operating System & Command Line Fundamentals
skill_quizzes.description: Permissions (chmod), process management, file inspection, piping, redirection, environment variables, and shell navigation.

questions.question: What does the command 'chmod 755 script.sh' accomplish?
options: Grants Read/Write/Execute to Owner (7), and Read/Execute to Group (5) and Others (5).
Grants all permissions to everyone in the world.
Deletes the file permanently after 755 seconds.
Encrypts the script with a 755-bit key.
questions.explanation: 7 (4+2+1=rwx) for owner, 5 (4+0+1=r-x) for group, 5 (r-x) for others.

questions.question: Which command is used to view active running processes in real-time with continuous updates?
options: top / htop
cat processes
ps -once
show all
questions.explanation: top (and htop) provides a dynamic real-time view of running system processes, CPU, and memory utilization.

questions.question: What is the difference between '>' and '>>' in Linux shell redirection?
options: '>' overwrites the destination file; '>>' appends output to the end of the destination file.
'>' appends; '>>' deletes the file.
'>' redirects standard error; '>>' redirects standard input.
There is no difference between them.
questions.explanation: '>' truncates/overwrites the target file with stdout; '>>' appends stdout to the file.

questions.question: Which command searches for a specific text pattern inside files using regular expressions?
options: grep
find
locate
cat
questions.explanation: grep (Global Regular Expression Print) searches text and prints matching lines.

questions.question: What does the pipe operator '|' do in Linux?
options: Redirects the standard output (stdout) of the preceding command into the standard input (stdin) of the succeeding command.
Executes both commands in parallel background threads.
Compares two files for textual equality.
Deletes intermediate error logs.
questions.explanation: Piping connects the output stream of one program directly into the input stream of another without writing to disk.

questions.question: What does the command 'kill -9 <PID>' do?
options: Sends the SIGKILL signal to immediately and forcefully terminate the process without cleanup.
Gracefully asks the process to exit after saving state (SIGTERM).
Pauses the process for 9 minutes.
Restarts the process with 9 threads.
questions.explanation: Signal 9 (SIGKILL) cannot be caught or ignored by a process, causing an immediate kernel termination.

questions.question: Which directory in standard Linux hierarchy holds global system configuration files?
options: /etc
/var
/bin
/tmp
questions.explanation: /etc contains configuration files and directories essential for system administration and daemon settings.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'sudo' command?
options: Executing a command with the security privileges of another user (by default, the superuser/root).
Switching the monitor resolution.
Downloading software packages from the web.
Rebooting the kernel immediately.
questions.explanation: sudo ('superuser do') permits authorized users to execute commands with elevated root security privileges.

questions.question: How do you view the last 50 lines of an application log file and keep following new incoming entries in real-time?
options: tail -n 50 -f app.log
head -n 50 app.log
cat app.log -follow
less app.log --top
questions.explanation: tail -f (or --follow) outputs appended data as the file grows; -n 50 specifies starting from the last 50 lines.

questions.question: What does 'chown user:group filename' do?
options: Changes the user owner and group owner of the specified file.
Changes file read/write permissions.
Renames the file to user:group.
Encrypts the file.
questions.explanation: chown (change owner) modifies the user and/or group ownership of filesystem items.

questions.question: Which command displays current disk space usage in human-readable units (GB, MB)?
options: df -h
du -all
free -m
ls -disk
questions.explanation: df -h (disk filesystem -human readable) displays total, used, and available space on mounted filesystems.

questions.question: What does 'cron' do in Linux?
options: A time-based job scheduling daemon that executes configured commands and scripts at specified intervals.
A text editor for writing C code.
A hardware diagnostic tool for checking RAM.
A network packet sniffer.
questions.explanation: Cron runs scheduled tasks (crontabs) periodically at fixed times, dates, or intervals.

questions.question: How do you set a persistent environment variable 'API_PORT=8080' for a bash user across shell restarts?
options: Add 'export API_PORT=8080' to ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile.
Type 'API_PORT=8080' in a temporary terminal and close it.
Create a file named /tmp/API_PORT.
Run 'chmod 8080 API_PORT'.
questions.explanation: Adding export KEY=VAL to ~/.bashrc ensures it is evaluated and loaded for every new interactive shell session.

questions.question: What does the command 'tar -czvf archive.tar.gz /path/to/folder' do?
options: Creates a gzip-compressed archive file of the specified folder.
Decompresses an existing zip file.
Deletes the folder after checking for viruses.
Uploads the folder to an FTP server.
questions.explanation: -c (create), -z (gzip), -v (verbose), -f (filename) packages and compresses a directory into an archive.

questions.question: What is the function of the command 'systemctl restart nginx'?
options: Restarts the Nginx systemd background service daemon.
Uninstalls Nginx from the operating system.
Changes Nginx server port to 80.
Reboots the physical machine.
questions.explanation: systemctl controls the systemd system and service manager to manage Linux background daemons.

questions.question: Which command creates a symbolic link (symlink) from target_file to link_name?
options: ln -s target_file link_name
link --sym target_file link_name
cp --link target_file link_name
alias target_file link_name
questions.explanation: ln -s creates a symbolic link that points to the target path without duplicating file data.

questions.question: What is standard error file descriptor number in Linux?
options: 0 (stdin)
1 (stdout)
questions.explanation: 0 is standard input (stdin), 1 is standard output (stdout), and 2 is standard error (stderr).

questions.question: What does '2>&1' mean in a shell command like 'command > output.log 2>&1'?
options: Redirects standard error (2) into the same destination as standard output (1).
Multiplies output by 2.
Reverses the command order.
Sends command to background thread 2.
questions.explanation: 2>&1 redirects file descriptor 2 (stderr) to file descriptor 1 (stdout), combining both streams into the output destination.

questions.question: Which command displays current memory (RAM) usage and swap space in megabytes?
options: free -m
mem -show
ram -v
top --ram
questions.explanation: free -m displays total, used, free, shared, and swap memory in megabytes.

questions.question: What does the command 'ssh-keygen -t ed25519' do?
options: Generates a modern, high-security Ed25519 public/private SSH key pair for passwordless authentication.
Decrypts an SSH password.
Deletes expired SSH certificates.
Opens a remote shell connection to a server.
questions.explanation: ssh-keygen creates an authentication key pair; Ed25519 is the modern elliptic-curve public-key algorithm.

skill_quizzes.name: Git & version control
skill_quizzes.description: Branching, merging vs rebasing, resolving conflicts, stash, commit history, pull/fetch, and Git workflows.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between 'git merge' and 'git rebase'?
options: Merge preserves complete historical commit graph and creates a merge commit; rebase rewrites project history by replaying commits atop the target branch.
Rebase deletes all commit messages.
Merge can only be used on the main branch; rebase works on feature branches.
Rebase requires network access to GitHub; merge operates offline.
questions.explanation: git merge combines branches with a dedicated merge commit preserving chronology; git rebase moves the feature branch base to maintain a linear history.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?
options: git fetch downloads remote commits without merging them into your working copy; git pull fetches and immediately attempts to merge (or rebase).
git pull only downloads tags.
git fetch deletes local untracked files.
There is no difference.
questions.explanation: git pull is essentially 'git fetch' followed immediately by 'git merge FETCH_HEAD'.

questions.question: What does 'git stash' do?
options: Temporarily shelves (stashes) uncommitted working directory changes so you can switch branches with a clean working tree.
Permanently deletes uncommitted files.
Pushes commits to the remote origin.
Creates an encrypted tag.
questions.explanation: git stash saves your dirty work-in-progress on a temporary stack and rolls back the working copy to HEAD.

questions.question: What does 'git reset --hard HEAD' do?
options: Discards all uncommitted changes in tracked files and resets both staging and working directory back to the latest commit.
Creates a backup commit.
Pushes changes to remote origin.
Merges origin/main into the branch.
questions.explanation: A hard reset discards all tracked working directory and index modifications, reverting files to the state of HEAD.

questions.question: What is the function of the '.gitignore' file?
options: Specifies intentionally untracked file patterns (e.g. node_modules, .env, build artifacts) that Git should ignore.
Stores Git user passwords.
Disables git push commands.
Configures the local text editor.
questions.explanation: .gitignore lists patterns matching files and directories that Git will not track or stage.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git revert <commit>' and 'git reset <commit>'?
options: git revert creates a brand new commit that inverts the changes of a previous commit; git reset moves the branch pointer backward, altering history.
git revert deletes the repository.
git reset can only be executed by repository administrators.
They are exact synonyms.
questions.explanation: git revert safely undoes changes in public shared branches without rewriting history; git reset alters the branch tip.

questions.question: What does the 'HEAD' pointer in Git represent?
options: A symbolic reference pointing to the currently checked-out commit and branch in the repository.
The head of the company engineering department.
The first commit ever made in the project.
The remote GitHub server address.
questions.explanation: HEAD is a pointer to the current snapshot and branch checked out in your working tree.

questions.question: What is a 'Merge Conflict' in Git?
options: A condition where two branches modify the same line of code differently, requiring manual resolution before completing the merge.
A network error between developer laptops.
A disk space outage on the server.
An expired SSH key.
questions.explanation: Conflicts occur when concurrent edits touch the same lines, preventing Git from automatically choosing which version to retain.

questions.question: What command allows you to view the commit history in a one-line concise format with an ASCII graph?
options: git log --oneline --graph
git show --tree
git history -graph
git commits -compact
questions.explanation: git log --oneline --graph draws an ASCII graph of branch and merge histories alongside compact commit hashes.

questions.question: What does 'git cherry-pick <commit-hash>' do?
options: Applies the changes introduced by a specific existing commit from another branch onto the current working branch as a new commit.
Deletes a commit from Git history.
Renames a branch.
Pushes one specific file to GitHub.
questions.explanation: Cherry-pick selects an individual commit from any branch and applies its diff directly onto your currently active HEAD.

questions.question: Which command stages all modified and newly created files in the current directory?
options: git add .
git stage all
git commit -a
git push --all
questions.explanation: git add . stages all changes in the current directory and subdirectories into the staging area (index).

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'git reflog'?
options: A safety ledger that records every movement of HEAD, allowing recovery of lost commits even after hard resets or rebase mistakes.
A list of remote repository contributors.
An error log file written by Git compiler.
A backup of deleted branches sent to an email.
questions.explanation: Reflog tracks local branch updates, enabling developers to restore orphaned commits that no branch currently points to.

questions.question: What is a 'Detached HEAD' state?
options: When HEAD points directly to a specific commit hash rather than to a named branch.
When the local repository is disconnected from the internet.
When Git deletes the master branch.
When a commit has no author email.
questions.explanation: Detached HEAD occurs when you checkout a specific commit directly; any new commits created will be orphaned unless a branch is created.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'git tag' (e.g. git tag -a v1.0.0)?
options: Creating an immutable named reference pointing to a specific commit, typically used to mark release milestones.
Labeling files by code syntax.
Assigning tasks to specific developers.
Marking duplicate commits for deletion.
questions.explanation: Tags mark specific points in repository history as important releases (v1.0.0, v2.1.0).

questions.question: Which command switches to an existing branch named 'feature-auth' in modern Git?
options: git switch feature-auth
git branch --change feature-auth
git move feature-auth
git update-branch feature-auth
questions.explanation: git switch branch_name was introduced to clearly separate branch navigation from file restoration (which git checkout previously overloaded).

questions.question: What does the command 'git diff --staged' show?
options: The differences between staged changes (in the index) and the latest commit (HEAD).
The differences between untracked files.
Differences between local and remote GitHub branches.
Changes made in other developer branches.
questions.explanation: git diff --staged (or --cached) inspects what will go into the next commit if you execute 'git commit'.

questions.question: What is a Git 'Fork' on hosting platforms like GitHub/GitLab?
options: A personal remote copy of another user's repository that allows you to freely experiment and submit pull requests.
A hardware tool used to reboot servers.
Splitting a single file into two parts.
A Git command built into the local command line.
questions.explanation: A fork is a server-side clone of a repository under your own account, enabling open-source contribution workflows via Pull Requests.

questions.question: What does 'git commit --amend' allow you to do?
options: Modify the most recent commit by adding new staged files or updating the commit message.
Undo the last 5 commits simultaneously.
Force push all branches to production.
Merge without conflict checks.
questions.explanation: git commit --amend combines staged changes with the immediately preceding commit, updating its contents and message.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'git clean -fd'?
options: Removes untracked files (-f) and untracked directories (-d) from the working tree.
Deletes Git history permanently.
Removes all comments from source code.
Cleans disk fragmentation.
questions.explanation: git clean deletes files and directories not tracked by Git, leaving only committed and ignored files.

questions.question: What is the standard format of a semantic Git commit message according to Conventional Commits?
options: <type>(<scope>): <short description> (e.g., feat(auth): add JWT login endpoint)
COMMIT #1: changes made today
Update files on Sunday
WIP
questions.explanation: Conventional Commits enforce structured prefixes (feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor) to enable automated changelogs and semver releases.

skill_quizzes.name: Python basics
skill_quizzes.description: Data types, mutability, list comprehensions, decorators, generators, error handling, and OOP.

questions.question: Which of the following built-in Python data types is mutable?
options: List
Tuple
String
Frozenset
questions.explanation: Lists can be modified in place (append, extend, pop); tuples, strings, and frozensets are immutable.

questions.question: What will the expression '[x**2 for x in range(5) if x % 2 == 0]' evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Even numbers in range(5) are 0, 2, 4. Their squares are 0, 4, 16.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'is' and '==' in Python?
options: 'is' checks for memory identity (same object in RAM); '==' checks for equality of values.
'==' is only for numbers; 'is' is only for strings.
'is' compares hash values; '==' compares lengths.
They are exact synonyms in Python 3.
questions.explanation: 'is' checks if id(a) == id(b); '==' invokes __eq__ to compare equality of contents.

questions.question: What does the 'yield' keyword do inside a Python function?
options: Turns the function into a Generator that yields values one at a time lazily, maintaining execution state.
Terminates the program immediately.
Imports an external C library.
Converts variables into global scope.
questions.explanation: yield pauses function execution and returns a generator iterator value, resuming on the next next() call.

questions.question: What is a Python Decorator?
options: A function that takes another function as an argument, extends its behavior without modifying it, and returns a function.
A syntax theme in VS Code.
A tool for creating desktop graphical windows.
An HTML tag used inside Python.
questions.explanation: Decorators (@decorator_name) wrap an existing function to execute pre- or post-processing logic cleanly.

questions.question: What do *args and **kwargs allow a function to accept in Python?
options: *args accepts variable positional arguments as a tuple; **kwargs accepts variable keyword arguments as a dictionary.
*args is for integers; **kwargs is for floating numbers.
*args imports modules; **kwargs deletes variables.
*args runs asynchronous code; **kwargs runs synchronous code.
questions.explanation: *args packs arbitrary positional parameters into a tuple; **kwargs packs arbitrary keyword arguments into a dict.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'finally' block in a try-except structure?
options: Code in 'finally' always executes regardless of whether an exception was raised or handled.
It only executes if no exceptions occurred.
It replaces the except block.
It runs only when an out-of-memory error happens.
questions.explanation: The 'finally' block executes cleanup operations (e.g., closing file descriptors or database sockets) unconditionally.

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy using the 'copy' module?
options: Shallow copy constructs a new object but references nested objects; deep copy recursively copies all nested objects.
Deep copy only works on strings.
Shallow copy deletes the original object.
They produce identical results on nested dictionaries.
questions.explanation: copy.copy() duplicates the outer container while inner elements remain shared; copy.deepcopy() duplicates the entire object hierarchy.

questions.question: What does the '__init__' method represent in a Python class?
options: The constructor / initializer method invoked automatically when a new instance of the class is instantiated.
A method that destroys class instances from RAM.
A private method that cannot be accessed by sub-classes.
A syntax validator for type hints.
questions.explanation: __init__ initializes attributes when an object is created from a class.

questions.question: What will 'bool([])' and 'bool([0])' return in Python?
options: False and True
True and False
False and False
True and True
questions.explanation: An empty list [] is falsy (False); a non-empty list [0] containing an element is truthy (True).

questions.question: How do you create a virtual environment in Python 3 using the standard library?
options: python -m venv myenv
python create env myenv
pip install virtualenv-all
python --make-virtual myenv
questions.explanation: 'python -m venv <dir>' creates an isolated Python installation environment.

questions.question: What is a Lambda function in Python?
options: A small, anonymous single-line function defined with the 'lambda' keyword.
A function that runs on AWS cloud only.
A function that cannot return any value.
A function imported from the math module.
questions.explanation: Lambda expressions define inline anonymous functions, e.g., lambda x, y: x + y.

questions.question: What will 'a = (1)' and 'b = (1,)' create respectively?
options: a is an integer (1); b is a single-element tuple (1,).
Both are tuples.
Both are integers.
a is a tuple; b is a syntax error.
questions.explanation: A trailing comma is mandatory to distinguish a single-element tuple from parenthesized integer arithmetic.

questions.question: What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in standard CPython?
options: A mutex lock that prevents multiple native threads from executing Python bytecodes simultaneously in one process.
A security firewall preventing unauthorized web access.
A database lock on SQL tables.
A lock on Git commit history.
questions.explanation: The GIL ensures thread-safe memory management in CPython by restricting bytecode execution to one thread at a time.

questions.question: What is the output of '"hello"[::-1]' in Python?
options: "olleh"
"hello"
questions.explanation: Slice notation [start:stop:step] with a step of -1 reverses the sequence.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'with' statement (Context Manager) in Python?
options: Ensures resources (like file streams and locks) are properly acquired and automatically released via __enter__ and __exit__.
Runs loops 10 times faster.
Creates a new thread.
Prevents syntax errors.
questions.explanation: 'with open(...) as f:' ensures files are closed automatically upon exiting the block, even if an exception occurs.

questions.question: Which dictionary method safely retrieves a value without raising a KeyError if the key is missing?
options: dict.get(key, default)
dict.fetch(key)
dict.find(key)
dict.lookup(key)
questions.explanation: dict.get('missing_key', default_val) returns None or the specified fallback value instead of raising a KeyError.

questions.question: What does 'pass' keyword represent in Python?
options: A null statement that serves as a syntactic placeholder where code is required but no action is taken.
Skips to the next iteration of a loop.
Returns True from a function.
Exits the application.
questions.explanation: 'pass' acts as a placeholder in empty functions, classes, or conditional branches.

questions.question: What is Method Resolution Order (MRO) in Python object-oriented programming?
options: The order in which Python searches for a method in a class hierarchy under multiple inheritance.
The order in which methods are compiled into bytecode.
The alphabetical sorting of class variables.
The speed of function execution.
questions.explanation: Python uses the C3 Linearization algorithm to determine the MRO order for attribute resolution in multiple inheritance.

questions.question: What does 'zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b'])' produce when converted to a list?
questions.explanation: zip pairs elements from each iterable into tuples at matching index positions.

skill_quizzes.name: JavaScript basics
skill_quizzes.description: Event loop, closures, promises, async/await, scope (let/const/var), prototype inheritance, and DOM.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between 'let' and 'var' in JavaScript?
options: 'let' is block-scoped and not hoisted with initialization; 'var' is function-scoped and hoisted with undefined.
'let' can be redeclared in the same scope; 'var' cannot.
'var' creates constants that cannot be reassigned.
'let' only works in browser environments, not Node.js.
questions.explanation: 'let' restricts scope to the containing { } block and prevents temporal dead zone errors; 'var' is function-scoped.
